Client economics: contribution, not headline revenue

Illustrative assumptions to replace with the client's actual records: $15,000 collected per additional roof; 30% contribution after direct job costs and sales commission = $4,500 per genuinely additional job. Full pilot fee $3,000 + software allowance $1,000 over 60 days + incremental client staff time $600 = $4,600 conservative total at full fee.

Genuinely additional roofsContributionAfter $4,600 pilot cost
0$0−$4,600
1$4,500−$100
2$9,000$4,400
3$13,500$8,900

Break-even is 1.023 additional jobs; in whole jobs, two. Five held conversations do not imply two incremental sales. If they would have bought anyway, count no incremental contribution. The payment remedy reduces cost if the conversation target is missed, but the client can still lose money even when it is met.

At only $2,000 contribution per job, three incremental roofs are needed at this budget. That is a materially harder case. Confirm actual margin and baseline follow-up before offering the pilot; do not use the headline contract value as ROI.

Agency economics and $20k/month

Internal planning assumptions, not contractor quotes: 32 hours across scoping, setup, QA and monitoring at $50/hour = $1,600; plus $200 internal overhead = $1,800. Full $3,000 revenue leaves $1,200 (40%) before acquisition, tax and uncosted owner work. If only the first $1,500 is earned, the pilot loses $300 before acquisition. This is a scoped learning pilot, not a 70%-margin claim.

Twenty continuing clients at $1,000/month is $20,000 recurring revenue—not profit. At four hours/client/month it is already 80 delivery hours before selling and management; eight hours/client doubles that. Seven $3,000 pilots is $21,000 total contract value, not necessarily cash collected this month and not recurring revenue. Scale only after measured outcomes and repeatable delivery.

How it would actually be delivered

  1. Scope and eligibility: confirm JobNimbus access, exact fields, quote age/status, contact permissions, rep ownership and baseline. No clean eligible cohort: no pilot.
  2. Start with the client's native capability: use what already works. If only basic reminders are missing, recommend that configuration rather than this service.
  3. Bounded integration if needed: JobNimbus records → workflow queue → approved SMS/email → incoming reply → AI-assisted classification/approved FAQ → human review or rep task → outcome sync. An implementation specialist must test exact read/write endpoints, rates, identity matching and permission profile in a sandbox.
  4. Initial supervised launch: test sample records and all stop/handoff cases, then review early replies before widening autonomy. Operator monitoring is part of delivery, not hidden manual labour.
  5. Weekly reconciliation: held reviews checked against rep outcomes; sold/lost/opt-outs reconciled; assess whether any wins were genuinely incremental. Use a small randomly chosen holdout when the cohort supports it, or label attribution observational.

JobNimbus API authentication and Twilio incoming-message webhooks support the integration route. They do not prove our integration has been built. No arbitrary CRM or universal connector promise.

Twilio's US pricing lists $0.0083 per inbound/outbound SMS segment before additional fees. At 2,000 segments that is $16.60 base usage—not the full stack cost. Registration, carrier fees, number, workflow hosting, AI, email, monitoring and CRM tier remain scope items. $500/month is a buyer-approved ceiling assumption, not a vendor quote. Do not assume an annual Hatch contract fits this 60-day pilot.

Twilio messaging policy requires appropriate consent and opt-out handling. The workflow excludes ineligible contacts. No scraped-homeowner SMS campaign is proposed.

Acquisition: how a student would find buyers

Start with owner-led calls and relevant, individually researched email to residential roofing companies in one chosen US metro. Build a small named list from contractor websites and trade directories, identify the owner/sales manager, and qualify quote volume and current process in conversation. CRM usage and open-estimate count cannot be inferred from a website.

Opening question: “When a replacement estimate is still open two weeks later, who owns getting the homeowner back on the phone?” Show the illustrative workflow, ask them to describe the last real stalled estimate, then assess pilot fit. Do not claim to have seen their private pipeline.

First experiment: ten owner conversations from an initial 50 researched companies; track whether the problem exists, qualification, current alternatives and willingness to pay. Those are experiment sizes, not forecast conversion rates. These four Meta ads are the next channel test once the message and cohort criteria survive those conversations. The eligible TAM has not been counted; no unsupported market-size claim is needed to assess this first pilot.

Checks and limits

Desktop/mobile rendering, horizontal overflow, all six storyboard scenes, qualification branches and eight PNG exports are checked separately from commercial quality. The form deliberately transmits nothing. No Base44 connector, sender, CRM account or real calendar is connected. This test delivers an offer and creative package; it does not deploy the service.
